content:
Regarding the dissolution of hereditary co-ownership between two siblings involving a single building, the Court addressed the concept of convenient divisibility under Article 720 of the Civil Code. While technically divisible, the property was deemed "not conveniently divisible" because partitioning would cause serious maintenance difficulties, create substandard units lacking essential services, and necessitate permanent co-ownership of the sole access point. The Court applied the principle that when division impairs the asset's utility or value, the property must be allocated in its entirety to the co-heir holding the majority share (2/3), who is then obligated to pay a monetary equalization (conguaglio) to the other party.
Furthermore, the Court clarified the procedural nature of accounting claims, such as requests for the reimbursement of hereditary debts or civil fruits (compensation for exclusive use). Under Articles 723 of the Civil Code and 166 of the Code of Civil Procedure, these claims are legally autonomous from the division request itself. The interpretative issue concerned whether such claims could be introduced at any stage; the Court ruled that they must be proposed in the introductory acts or within strict statutory deadlines. Consequently, the principle applied is that a claim for fruits is inadmissible if filed late, as it impermissibly expands the thema decidendum and introduces new investigative themes.
